differential: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Young patient with chronic bronchitis, which is one of the two main forms of COPD, though unusual at this age without smoking history.
Asthma
Can present with chronic respiratory symptoms and bronchial inflammation that may be characterized as chronic bronchitis by the patient.
Bronchiectasis
Causes chronic productive cough and recurrent bronchial infections that could be described as chronic bronchitis.
Cystic fibrosis
Should be considered in a young adult with chronic bronchitis, as it causes chronic pulmonary disease with recurrent infections.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Rare genetic cause of early-onset COPD/chronic bronchitis in young non-smokers or minimal smokers.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out diagnoses without further history, examination findings, or diagnostic testing.

differential: Chronic bronchitis
History of chronic bronchitis with mild rhonchi on exam is consistent with ongoing airway inflammation and mucus production.
Asthma
Chronic airway inflammation can present with rhonchi and may have been previously misdiagnosed as chronic bronchitis in a young patient.
Bronchiectasis
Can present with chronic productive cough and rhonchi, often develops secondary to recurrent infections or inflammation.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
Can cause chronic respiratory symptoms and bronchitis-like presentation through microaspiration and vagal irritation.
Post-infectious bronchial hyperreactivity
May cause persistent rhonchi and bronchitis symptoms following respiratory infection in an otherwise healthy young adult.
eliminated: Acute bronchitis
Normal vital signs and routine checkup context suggest chronic rather than acute process.
Pneumonia
Absence of fever, normal vital signs, and only mild scattered rhonchi make acute infection unlikely.

differential: Chronic bronchitis with vitamin K deficiency
Young patient with confirmed chronic bronchitis and isolated PT prolongation suggesting vitamin K deficiency from malabsorption or poor nutrition.
Cystic fibrosis
Chronic bronchitis in young adult with bronchial thickening on imaging and prolonged PT from fat-malabsorption causing vitamin K deficiency.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia
Chronic respiratory symptoms from childhood with bronchial thickening, though PT prolongation would require concurrent nutritional deficiency.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
Chronic bronchitis with radiographic changes, though unusual age for COPD unless alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency present.
Occult liver disease
Prolonged PT from hepatic synthetic dysfunction with chronic bronchitis as separate or related condition (e.g., alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency).
eliminated: Acute bronchitis
History indicates chronic rather than acute condition with structural changes on chest x-ray.
Warfarin use/anticoagulation
No mention of anticoagulant therapy in history and patient presents for routine checkup.

differential: Cystic fibrosis
Confirmed by genetic testing with classic features of chronic bronchitis, fat malabsorption (steatorrhea), and vitamin K deficiency causing prolonged PT.
Pancreatic insufficiency secondary to cystic fibrosis
The steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency directly indicate exocrine pancreatic dysfunction from CF.
Chronic pancreatitis
Could cause fat malabsorption and vitamin K deficiency with steatorrhea, though less likely given genetic confirmation of CF and young age.
Celiac disease
Can cause fat malabsorption and vitamin K deficiency, but genetic testing confirmed CF as the underlying cause.
Primary biliary cholangitis
Could theoretically cause fat malabsorption and vitamin K deficiency, but extremely unlikely given age, genetic CF diagnosis, and lack of cholestatic features.
eliminated: Warfarin use/coagulopathy of other cause
Prolonged PT explained by vitamin K deficiency from fat malabsorption, not primary coagulation disorder.
Isolated vitamin K deficiency from dietary causes
The multisystem involvement with bronchitis, steatorrhea, and genetic confirmation points to CF as the underlying cause.
Simple chronic bronchitis
The combination of pulmonary disease, pancreatic insufficiency, and genetic testing confirms this is manifestation of CF, not isolated bronchitis.

differential: Chronic bronchitis secondary to smoking
Most common cause of chronic bronchitis in young adults is cigarette smoking.
Asthma with chronic bronchitic component
Young female with chronic airway inflammation may have underlying asthma presenting as chronic bronchitis.
Chronic bronchitis secondary to occupational/environmental exposure
Prolonged exposure to dust, fumes, or pollutants can cause chronic bronchitis in young adults.
Bronchiectasis
Chronic productive cough and recurrent infections may indicate underlying bronchiectasis causing bronchitic symptoms.
Cystic fibrosis (mild variant)
Young adult with chronic bronchitis should be evaluated for underlying CF, particularly if incompletely diagnosed previously.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out diagnoses.

differential: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
Young female with petechiae and bruising suggesting isolated thrombocytopenia without other systemic findings.
Acute leukemia
Petechiae and bruising from thrombocytopenia with possible bone marrow infiltration, though lack of other systemic symptoms is atypical.
Aplastic anemia
Petechiae and bruising from pancytopenia, though isolated thrombocytopenia more common initially.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)
Petechiae and bruising from microangiopathic process, though lack of fever, neurologic symptoms, or renal dysfunction is unusual.
Medication-induced thrombocytopenia
Petechiae and bruising from drug effect, possibly related to medications for chronic bronchitis or other unmentioned drugs.
eliminated: Chronic bronchitis exacerbation
Lung auscultation is clear with no respiratory symptoms reported at this visit.

differential: Vitamin K deficiency
Prolonged PT with bruising and petechiae suggests impaired synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).
Liver disease/cirrhosis
Hepatic dysfunction can cause prolonged PT due to decreased synthesis of clotting factors and manifest with easy bruising.
Warfarin/anticoagulant use
Prolonged PT with bleeding manifestations (bruising, petechiae) is classic for warfarin therapy or surreptitious anticoagulant ingestion.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Can present with prolonged PT and bleeding manifestations, though typically more acute and severe than described here.
Factor VII deficiency
Isolated factor VII deficiency causes isolated PT prolongation with bleeding tendency (bruising and petechiae).
eliminated: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)
Would not cause prolonged PT; affects platelet count and PTT typically remains normal.
Hemophilia A or B
These cause prolonged PTT, not PT, and are X-linked conditions rarely symptomatic in females.

differential: Cystic fibrosis
Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis, explaining chronic bronchitis, malabsorption with steatorrhea, and vitamin K deficiency causing coagulopathy and bleeding manifestations.
Pancreatic insufficiency secondary to cystic fibrosis
Steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption directly result from exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, a major complication of cystic fibrosis.
Vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy
Prolonged PT, bruising, and petechiae are directly caused by documented vitamin K deficiency from fat malabsorption in cystic fibrosis.
Chronic pancreatitis
Could cause similar malabsorption and steatorrhea, though genetic confirmation of cystic fibrosis makes this a secondary or related process rather than primary diagnosis.
Malabsorption syndrome
While cystic fibrosis is the underlying cause, this describes the clinical syndrome of fat malabsorption manifesting as steatorrhea and vitamin deficiencies.
eliminated: Primary coagulation disorder (e.g., hemophilia, von Willebrand disease)
Normal aPTT expected and isolated PT prolongation with low vitamin K explains the coagulopathy.
Liver disease
Normal metabolic function and selective vitamin K deficiency without other liver dysfunction markers makes this unlikely.
Celiac disease
Genetic testing confirmed cystic fibrosis as the cause of malabsorption.
Inflammatory bowel disease
Steatorrhea pattern and confirmed cystic fibrosis explain the gastrointestinal symptoms.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The physical exam reveals multiple bruises and petechiae, which argues against chronic Vitamin K deficiency, which would not typically present without a clear bleeding diathesis.
